newsitem.title: USA: US Airways says growth remains on hold.
newsitem.headline: US Airways says growth remains on hold.

text.p: US Airways Group Inc's dream of building a stronger, global airline "remains on hold," so the company must now focus on becoming a smaller, regional carrier, Chairman Stephen Wolf said Wednesday.
In a search for new ways to build shareholder value, US Airways will consider diverting some funds to buy regional jets for its commuter subsidiaries, he said.
"We remain at a crossroads," Wolf told shareholders at the company's annual meeting in Philadelphia.

Since it has yet to reach a cost-cutting agreement with unionized employees, US Airways' expansion plans have stalled. Hanging in the balance is an order for up to 400 Airbus wide-body jets, build a midwestern hub and launch a low- cost service to compete with rivals such as Southwest Airlines Co .
"We find no choice but to focus on being a smaller carrier," Wolf said.
US Airways, which has among the highest costs in the airline industry, recently announced plans to cut some unprofitable routes, consolidate facilities and reduce its fleet.
US Airways said it will now look for new ways to use the money it had amassed in preparation for its growth plan.
On Tuesday, the company said it plans to spend $126.2 million to buy back some shares of US Airways preferred stock now held by its estranged marketing partner British Airways Plc.
That deal will reduce US Airways' shares outstanding and eliminate $27 million in annual preferred dividend costs.
"One of the things we started to do was build cash...as part of our long-term plan. We've been stopped from doing that. Now we're using that cash to build shareholder value," Wolf said.
"We will also be open to put in place a (plan to be a) global competitor. But we have a fidiciary responsibility to pursue other alternatives," Wolf said.

US Airways said Wednesday it is in talks with aircraft manufacturers to buy an unspecified number of regional aircraft. The new jets would be flown by its commuter subsidiaries, not by the main airline.
Wolf said the company previously had no interest in buying regional jet, since it had wanted to use its funds to buy larger aircraft for its main operations.
"We did not envision allocating funds to regional jets," Wolf said.
While many industry analysts said the company's recent downsizing plans were long overdue, other analysts suggested the company is also posturing with its pilots union.

"We're in the biggest boom the domestic airline industry has seen. How can they justify downsizing the airline?" said Jon Bryan, chairman of the US Airways unit of the Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA).
"Management previously said 'Why would we spend many millions of dollars on regional jets when we could buy Airbus (planes).' It makes no sense," Bryan said.

Pilots union members appeared at the company's annual meeting in droves and urged the company to resume contract negotiations on a full-time basis. The company recently shifted some of its negotating resources away from the pilots in order to focus on contract negotiations with other labor groups.
But Wolf said that after years of contract negotiations, "It's a matter of will to implement a competitive cost structure, not a matter of hours of negotiating."

The Air Line Pilots Association has offered the company a plan to cut costs and develop at unit to compete with low-cost carriers. The two sides disagree on the size and scope of the proposed low-cost unit.
